n: Paul appeals to everything they have received: if Christ has ever encouraged you, if love has comforted you, if the Spirit has bound you together, if you have felt tenderness and mercy — then act on it.

f.g: Tender affections and compassion.

n: Make my joy complete by being united: one in love, one in heart, one in purpose. Unity among the Saints was Paul’s greatest wish for this beloved branch.

f.g: Literally “one-souled” — united in heart.

n: Don’t act out of rivalry or a desire to look important. Instead, humbly treat others as more important than yourself.

f.g: Empty conceit, seeking praise for oneself.
Humility.

n: Don’t look out only for your own interests; care about other people’s needs too. This sets up Paul’s great example of Christ.
Have the same attitude Jesus had. Verses 6–11 are often called the “Christ hymn” — many scholars think it was an early Christian hymn or poem Paul quotes.

f.w: Let this mind be in you
f.g: Think the way Christ thought; adopt His attitude.

n: Though Christ shared the divine nature with the Father in the premortal life, He did not cling to that status as something to hold onto for Himself.

f.g: Greek morphē — true nature, not just outward look.
Something to grasp or cling to. Christ’s equality with God was rightly His, yet He did not grasp it selfishly.

n: Instead He emptied Himself, taking the lowly role of a servant and being born as a human being. Latter-day Saints call this the condescension of God.

f.g: Greek ekenōsen — “emptied himself.”

n: As a man, He humbled Himself even further — obeying the Father all the way to death, and not just any death, but crucifixion, the most shameful execution Rome used.

f.g: Crucifixion was reserved for slaves and rebels; it was meant to shame.

n: Because of that humility, the Father lifted Christ to the highest place and gave Him the greatest of all names. The way down became the way up.

f.w: a name which is above every name

n: Every being — in heaven, on earth, and among the dead — will eventually bow before Jesus. Paul is echoing Isaiah, where Jehovah says every knee shall bow to Him.
And everyone will acknowledge that Jesus Christ is Lord, which brings glory to the Father. Christ’s exaltation honors the Father rather than competing with Him.

f.g: Greek kyrios — the word the Greek Old Testament used for Jehovah.

n: So, just as you have always obeyed, keep at it even more now that I’m not there: work out your salvation with reverent seriousness. Salvation is a gift, but disciples must actively live it out.

f.g: Deep reverence and humility, not terror.

n: You are not working alone — God is working in you, giving you both the desire and the power to do what pleases Him. Our effort and His grace work together.

f.w: both to will and to do

n: Do everything without grumbling or arguing. Complaining divides communities, and Paul wants this branch united.
Then you will be pure and innocent children of God, shining like stars in a dark and twisted world. Paul echoes Moses’s words about a crooked generation.
Hold out the life-giving message of the gospel to others. Then, at Christ’s coming, Paul can rejoice that his efforts — his race and labor — were not wasted.
Even if Paul’s life is poured out like a drink offering on top of their faith-offering, he is glad. He pictures his possible death as a sacrifice added to theirs.

f.g: Greek spendomai — poured out like a drink offering (libation) on a sacrifice.

n: Paul invites them to share his joy rather than mourn for him. Rejoicing together becomes a bond between them.
Paul hopes, if the Lord wills, to send Timothy soon so that he can hear how they are doing and be encouraged by good news.

f.g: Greek form of Timothy.
How you are doing; your circumstances.

n: No one else shares Paul’s heart the way Timothy does, or cares so genuinely for their welfare.

f.g: Literally “equal-souled” — of the same spirit.

n: Paul laments that most people are focused on their own concerns rather than on Christ’s work. Timothy is a happy exception.
The Philippians already know Timothy’s proven character; he has served alongside Paul like a son working with his father.

f.g: Proven worth, tested character.

f.w: as a son with the father

n: Paul plans to send Timothy as soon as he learns the outcome of his own trial.

f.g: Immediately, at once.

n: Paul trusts the Lord that he himself will soon be released and come visit them.
Meanwhile, he is sending Epaphroditus — a Philippian whom the branch had sent to bring Paul gifts and care for him. Paul honors him with three titles: brother, co-worker, and fellow soldier.

f.g: Greek apostolos — one sent on a mission.

n: Epaphroditus was homesick and distressed — not about his own illness, but because the Philippians had heard about it and would worry.

f.g: Distress, deep anxiety.

n: He had nearly died. But God showed mercy by healing him, sparing Paul from adding grief upon grief to his imprisonment.

f.g: Near.

n: So Paul is sending him home eagerly, so the Philippians can rejoice to see him well and Paul can have one less worry.

f.g: Eagerly, with haste.

n: Welcome him joyfully as a brother in the Lord, and honor people like him who serve so selflessly.

f.g: Esteem such people highly.

n: He risked his life doing Christ’s work, filling in the service the Philippians could not give in person because they were far away.

f.g: Some manuscripts read “gambling with his life.”
What you were unable to do yourselves because of distance — not a criticism.
